strengths: The paper investigates a relevant connection between polysemantic representations and model robustness, combining feature-, token-, prompt-, and neuron-level interventions into a coherent exploratory study.

The prompt experiments provide a concrete empirical signal across four models. For example, high-interference prefixes achieve 27.64% versus 20.33% success for random prefixes on LLaMA location targets, and 26.68% versus 15.45% on Gemma. Comparisons with low-interference and direct-target prefixes help contextualize these effects.

The appendices provide dataset-generation prompts, additional experimental repetitions, and illustrative interventions. The paper also acknowledges SAE instability and the limitations of next-token evaluation.
weaknesses: The activation-intervention evaluation is substantially biased by outcome-dependent selection. Appendix F.2 explicitly excludes results when outputs align more with the interference feature than with the target, removing a central failure mode. It also selects the best intervention strength separately for each evaluation sentence. Without unconditional results, exclusion rates, and held-out strength selection, the reported averages establish neither typical effectiveness nor generalization.

The claimed black-box transfer conflates different access assumptions. Appendix H.2 computes gradients and modifies residual activations inside LLaMA, which requires white-box access; lacking a pretrained SAE does not make this black-box. Only the prompt intervention supports a black-box interpretation. The headline claim of over 95% gradient-intervention success also lacks a sufficiently specified aggregate evaluation and matched baselines.

The experiments do not establish that transferable polysemantic topology causes the observed effects. Transfer of selected tokens can arise from shared lexical associations, token frequency, punctuation, or contextual priming. Appendix H.2 acknowledges that many selected tokens are punctuation or have everyday associations with targets. Frequency-, semantic-, and token-type-matched controls, together with causal feature measurements in recipient models, are needed before asserting persistent topology or challenging alternative theories of polysemanticity.

The metrics do not reliably measure the intended semantic intervention. Absolute Kendall and Spearman correlations reward reversed rankings as strongly as correct rankings, and correlations over small token-set intersections can be unstable. Embedding proximity can also conflate antonyms: grouping love and hate cannot demonstrate controlled sentiment polarity. Table 1 even presents increased probabilities of 'grateful', 'blessed', and 'excited' as an intervention targeting sadness.

The safety and covert-manipulation claims exceed the evaluation. Experiments primarily measure top-10 next-token changes in synthetic contexts deliberately constructed to favor target tokens. They do not demonstrate downstream factual errors, harmful compliance, sustained generation changes, preserved fluency, or reduced detectability. The reported prompt effects are interesting sensitivity results, but their practical safety significance remains unestablished.

The neuron-polysemanticity findings have unresolved measurement and intervention confounds. Cluster counts depend on unvalidated semantic clustering, connection thresholds, and restricting attention to three coordinates per cluster. Multiplicative interventions are not matched for activation magnitude or perturbation norm, while suppression and amplification use markedly different ranges. Thus, greater effects and 'super-neuron' asymmetry could reflect activation scale or generic neuron importance rather than polysemanticity.

Important methodological details are inconsistent or missing. Appendix G.1 defines an input-embedding gradient of a linear activation probe with unspecified vector v, whereas G.2 describes gradients of a token with respect to layer neurons; these are different procedures. Feature sample counts are reversed between the main text and Appendix F.2. Semantic embedding and cluster-aggregation details are insufficiently specified, and the statistical reporting does not explain how dependence among repeated injections on the same prompts is handled. These issues impede reproduction and assessment of the reported significance.

strengths: The paper investigates a relevant question at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and robustness: whether semantically distinct but geometrically overlapping features enable unintended steering.

The experiments cover feature, token-gradient, prompt, and neuron interventions, with random, low-interference, and direct-target comparisons. Appendix replications provide some evidence that the observed effects are repeatable.

Table 2 provides evidence that SAE-informed token selection improves prompt steering over random selection across four models. For location targets, success rates improve from 20.33% to 27.64% on LLaMA and from 15.45% to 26.68% on Gemma.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic interpretation is not established. Transfer of selected tokens does not demonstrate preservation of polysemantic topology across models; shared lexical associations, token frequency, and ordinary contextual priming remain plausible explanations. Appendix H.2 acknowledges contextual relationships between interference and target tokens. Frequency-, syntax-, and semantic-association-matched controls, together with direct measurements of target-model representations, are needed.

The black-box characterization is incorrect for the gradient interventions. Appendix H.2 explicitly computes gradients and modifies residual-layer activations inside LLaMA. Not requiring a pretrained SAE does not make an intervention black-box. This materially overstates the access assumptions and transfer results in the abstract, Finding 4, and conclusion.

The evaluation uses substantial outcome-dependent selection. Appendix F.2 excludes interventions whose outputs align more strongly with the interference feature than the target and selects the best steering coefficient separately for each evaluated sentence. Appendix H.3 also reports best improvements. Without exclusion rates, unconditional results, and held-out evaluation of fixed intervention choices, these results cannot establish reliable intervention effectiveness.

The metrics do not consistently measure the claimed semantic effect. Absolute Kendall and Spearman correlations reward reversed rankings, and correlations on small token-set intersections can be unstable or undefined without a specified handling rule. Grouping hate and love also cannot establish control over sentiment polarity. Table 1 illustrates this mismatch: an intervention targeting sadness increases grateful, blessed, and excited while decreasing bad and guilty.

The safety and covertness claims substantially exceed the evidence. Evaluation primarily measures top-10 next-token changes on synthetic prompts deliberately constructed to accommodate the target token. There are no demonstrated policy violations, downstream factual failures, sustained generation effects, or measurements of detectability and fluency. The results support local steering sensitivity more directly than practical covert vulnerabilities.

The neuron analysis does not isolate polysemanticity from other determinants of intervention sensitivity. Feature counts depend on clustering, a connection threshold, and top-three-neuron selection, without sensitivity analyses or controls for activation magnitude, layer, or decoder loading. Moreover, suppression scales activations between zero and one while amplification extends to twenty, so the reported asymmetry needs perturbation-magnitude-matched controls.

Important implementation details are inconsistent or underspecified. Appendix G.1 defines a gradient of an activation projection with respect to input embeddings, whereas G.2 describes gradients of a token with respect to layer neurons; the projection vector and relationship between these procedures remain unclear. Main-text and appendix target-feature counts are reversed between models. Semantic embedding and clustering details are insufficient, and the manuscript states that code is available without supplying an accessible link.

Overall, the empirical steering effects are promising exploratory observations, but the unresolved selection bias, access-model mischaracterization, and unsupported causal interpretation leave the contribution below the acceptance standard for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper investigates a relevant question at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and model robustness: whether semantically distinct but geometrically overlapping features permit indirect behavioral interventions.

The experiments cover feature, token-gradient, prompt, and neuron interventions, with random, low-interference, and direct-target comparisons. Appendix replications provide additional evidence beyond selected examples.

The prompt-transfer results are promising. In Table 2, high-interference prefixes outperform random prefixes on both larger models; for locations, success increases from 20.33% to 27.64% on LLaMA and from 15.45% to 26.68% on Gemma.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic conclusion exceeds the evidence. Transfer of token prefixes does not establish a shared polysemantic topology: ordinary linguistic associations, token frequency, punctuation, and shared training distributions could explain transfer. Appendix H.2 acknowledges that interference tokens often include punctuation or contextually related words. Matched controls and causal mediation through the hypothesized features are needed to distinguish these explanations.

The intervention evaluation contains substantial selection bias. Appendix F.2 excludes outcomes when the output is more similar to the interference feature than the target feature, removing precisely an important failure mode. It also selects the best steering scale for each evaluated sentence, without a reported held-out selection protocol. Consequently, the reported averages describe filtered, oracle-tuned effects rather than reliable intervention performance. Unfiltered results, exclusion rates, and held-out evaluation are necessary.

The black-box claim is incorrect for the gradient-based experiments. Appendix H.2 explicitly computes gradients and intervenes on LLaMA residual layers, requiring internal access. The discussion acknowledges this requirement but still describes these interventions as black-box and possible without internal weights. Only the prompt-based experiments support that access setting; the headline claim of over 95% gradient-steering success also lacks a sufficiently detailed aggregate evaluation and matched baseline.

The metrics do not reliably establish the claimed semantic control. Absolute Kendall and Spearman correlations treat reversed rankings as strong agreement, and correlations over small top-10 intersections can be unstable. Embedding similarity can conflate antonyms: Table 1 labels a target as sadness while the intervention increases 'grateful', 'blessed', and 'excited'. Grouping hate and love similarly does not demonstrate control over sentiment polarity. Direct target probabilities, signed semantic judgments, and generated-continuation evaluation would be more convincing.

The safety and covertness claims are insufficiently evaluated. The experiments primarily measure next-token changes on synthetic sentence fragments deliberately constructed to accommodate the target. They do not demonstrate factual errors, harmful compliance, sustained behavioral changes, or concealment from a detector or human observer. Fluency and task preservation are not measured, despite steering scales reaching 20.

The neuron-level analysis does not isolate polysemanticity from ordinary neuron importance. Connection counts depend on arbitrary clustering and weight thresholds, without sensitivity analyses or controls for activation magnitude, decoder norms, layer, and downstream influence. Comparing suppression factors in [0,1] with amplification up to 20 also makes the reported asymmetry difficult to interpret without matched perturbation magnitudes.

Important methodological details remain ambiguous. Appendix G.1 defines gradients of a projected hidden activation with respect to input embeddings, whereas G.2 describes gradients of a token with respect to layer neurons; the projection vector and relationship between these procedures are not adequately specified. Semantic embedding and clustering choices are also insufficiently documented, and the main text and Appendix F.2 reverse the per-model target-feature sample counts. These issues materially hinder reproduction.

strengths: The paper investigates a relevant question: whether interference between apparently unrelated SAE features predicts behavioral effects across models. Combining feature, token, prompt, and neuron interventions provides useful exploratory breadth.

The feature-direction experiments report consistent relationships between decoder-direction similarity and intervention effectiveness, with random and direct-target baselines, multiple semantic thresholds, and regression controls.

Robustness checks include an alternative probability-mass metric, a second feature interpreter on one layer, and additional transfer categories. Reporting unsuccessful transfer cases in Appendix K is valuable.
weaknesses: The central black-box claim is incorrect for token-gradient interventions. Appendix K.1 explicitly computes gradients and modifies residual activations inside Llama, requiring target-model internal access. Absence of a pretrained SAE does not make this black-box access. This distinction materially weakens the headline contribution and the interpretation of the reported greater-than-95% success rate.

Transfer of a shared polysemantic structure is not established. Appendix K uses the union of interference-token sets from the small models, rather than requiring agreement between them. There are no comparisons against single-source selection or matched nonshared structures. Successful transfer of token associations alone does not demonstrate preservation of the underlying interference topology in larger models.

The genuinely black-box prompt results are modest and inconsistent. In Table 1, high-interference tokens underperform low-interference tokens for numbers on both small models, Llama-8B, and Gemma; several settings also fail to outperform random tokens. Significance tests compare against random, not the crucial high-versus-low contrast. Appendix K states that the three main-text categories were selected for strong generalizability from eight tested categories, weakening claims of reliable transfer.

The evaluation reports oracle-tuned intervention effects. Appendix H.2 selects the scaling coefficient that maximizes each metric on each evaluated sentence, without a held-out tuning protocol. Restricting the coefficient range does not establish output coherence or preserved capability. Appendix L acknowledges likely substantial impairment at the original strengths; even after reducing strength fourfold, 149 of 174 vectors reduce HellaSwag accuracy. Selected favorable examples do not establish a general effectiveness–utility tradeoff.

The causal attribution to polysemanticity is insufficiently isolated. Decoder cosine similarity measures geometric overlap, and perturbing overlapping directions can produce related effects without establishing the proposed mechanism. Gloss-embedding dissimilarity does not exclude lexical overlap, contextual association, or shared training statistics. Frequency-, syntax-, and association-matched token controls and direct measurements of target-feature mediation are missing. The paired-choice annotation result, where high-interference pairs are judged more related 64.3% of the time, leaves semantic association as a plausible explanation.

Important methodological details are inconsistent or underspecified. Section 3.2 describes gradients of tokens with respect to layer neurons, whereas Appendix I.1 defines gradients of a projected activation with respect to input embeddings and leaves the projection vector v unspecified. How these directions are injected or transported in the actual experiments is unclear. The neuron analysis also lacks controls for activation magnitude, connection strength, and layer, so greater sensitivity cannot confidently be attributed to feature count.

The evidence supports a narrower exploratory finding than the paper's claims about vulnerabilities, latent knowledge, and human cognition. Most outcomes concern next-token rankings on synthetic contexts already designed to elicit the target category; sustained behavioral control or safety-policy violations are not demonstrated. Automated annotators' failure to identify associations does not establish human unintelligibility, particularly given their low agreement. These unresolved interpretation and evaluation issues place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper investigates a relevant question: whether interference between apparently unrelated SAE features can predict transferable behavioral effects. Connecting representation geometry to interventions across model families is potentially valuable.

The experimental scope includes four intervention types, two small source models, and three larger instruction-tuned models. Feature-direction interventions provide evidence that greater decoder-direction similarity is associated with stronger target-token effects.

Useful robustness checks include multiple semantic-similarity thresholds, an alternative probability-mass metric, controlled regressions, and a second feature annotator on one layer. The appendices also disclose unsuccessful transfer categories and downstream performance degradation.
weaknesses: The central black-box claim is materially inaccurate for token-gradient steering. Appendix K.1 explicitly computes gradients and modifies residual layers inside Llama, and Section 4 acknowledges the need for internal activations. Not requiring a pretrained SAE does not make an intervention black-box. The reported greater-than-95% gradient-steering success therefore cannot support the advertised control without access to model internals.

Behavioral transfer does not establish preservation of polysemantic topology. Appendix K constructs unions of interference-token sets from the source models, rather than requiring an interference relationship to hold in both. The paper lacks source-specific versus shared-set ablations and direct confirmation of the proposed relationships in destination models. Shared lexical associations or training-data regularities remain plausible explanations.

The actual prompt-transfer evidence is mixed and often modest. In Table 1, high-interference tokens underperform low-interference tokens for number targets on both Llama-8B and Gemma-9B, while several other comparisons show little benefit over random. Appendix K.2 explicitly identifies the three main-text categories as those with strong generalizability and reports five additional categories separately. Significance against random does not establish superiority over low interference; direct paired comparisons and a complete aggregate analysis are needed.

The steering evaluation uses oracle selection on the evaluation examples. Appendix H.2 selects the scale giving the greatest metric improvement separately for each sentence, without a held-out tuning protocol. These results characterize optimized intervention potential rather than a fixed, predictively transferable intervention. The claimed preservation of coherence is also unsupported by a quantitative constraint: Appendix L acknowledges likely substantial impairment at the original strengths and reports accuracy degradation for 149 of 174 vectors even after reducing their strength.

The operational definitions do not isolate polysemantic interference convincingly. Decoder cosine similarity measures geometric overlap, while similarity between automatically generated gloss embeddings is an imperfect proxy for semantic unrelatedness. Steering with overlapping directions can affect similar outputs without establishing the proposed mechanism. Frequency-, lexical-overlap-, semantic-association-, and perturbation-norm-matched controls, together with causal measurements of target-feature activation, would strengthen the attribution. The comparatively flat gradient-steering results further weaken interference magnitude as the explanation for that method.

The evaluation is dominated by immediate next-token changes on synthetic contexts explicitly constructed to invite the target token or category. Entering a top-30 list does not establish reliable generated behavior, covert manipulation, or a safety failure. The 500-example HellaSwag check measures collateral accuracy effects and presents selected successful examples, but does not provide a systematic downstream target-control versus utility tradeoff.

Important methodological details remain ambiguous. Section 3.2 describes a gradient with respect to layer neurons, whereas Appendix I.1 defines an input-embedding gradient using an unspecified projection vector v. How that vector is chosen and injected is insufficiently explained. Confidence intervals and significance tests also need an explicit treatment of dependence among repeated prompts, shared features, and layers.

The broader interpretations exceed the evidence. Automatic annotators have limited agreement, and their failure to identify an association does not establish that it is opaque to humans. Indeed, the paired-choice test selects high-interference pairs as more semantically related 64.3% of the time, suggesting residual semantic confounding. Likewise, neuron sensitivity is not controlled for activation magnitude or weight norms, so the claimed special role of highly polysemantic 'super-neurons' remains preliminary.

strengths: The paper investigates a relevant interpretability question: whether semantically dissimilar SAE features exhibit interference that predicts intervention effects across models. Connecting representation geometry to transferable behavioral changes is potentially valuable.

The experiments cover four intervention types, two small source models, and three larger instruction-tuned models. Feature-direction experiments provide evidence that greater decoder-direction similarity predicts stronger steering effects.

Useful robustness checks include multiple semantic-similarity thresholds, an alternative probability-mass metric, regression controls, and feature descriptions from a second annotator. The appendices also report unsuccessful transfer categories, which helps assess the findings.
weaknesses: The central claim of black-box transfer is overstated. Section 3.4 treats token-gradient steering as requiring no internal access, but Appendix K.1 explicitly computes gradients and modifies residual layers in the destination model. This demonstrates transfer of intervention-text selection with white-box destination access, not black-box steering. The discussion partially acknowledges this requirement but continues to claim black-box transfer through both methods.

The genuinely black-box prompt results provide limited evidence for transferable interference structure. In Table 1, high-interference tokens sometimes underperform low-interference or random tokens; for GPT-2 number targets, the rates are 30.33%, 31.23%, and 34.71%, respectively. Appendix K.2 states that the three main-text categories were selected for strong generalizability, while five others transfer less consistently. Significance tests compare against random tokens rather than directly establishing the crucial high-versus-low interference difference.

The transfer construction does not isolate the claimed shared structure. Appendix K uses the union of source-model token sets, which need not contain interference patterns present in both models. Comparisons against intersection-based selection, each source alone, and token-frequency or contextual-association matched controls are needed to establish that shared polysemantic geometry explains transfer.

The steering evaluation reports optimistic per-example upper bounds. Appendix H.2 selects the scale giving the greatest metric improvement separately for each evaluation sentence, without a held-out tuning protocol. There is also no quantitative coherence constraint supporting repeated claims that interventions preserve model behavior. Appendix L acknowledges likely substantial impairment at the original scales; even after reducing strength, 149 of 174 vectors decrease HellaSwag accuracy. Selected favorable examples do not establish a reliable control–utility tradeoff.

The evidence does not establish the proposed mechanism as strongly as claimed. Low similarity between embeddings of automatically generated glosses does not establish semantic independence, and decoder-vector overlap is a geometric proxy rather than direct evidence of causal feature interference. The paired-choice experiment finds high-interference pairs more semantically related 64.3% of the time, indicating residual semantic association. LLM annotators failing to identify relationships cannot establish that those relationships are opaque to human intuition or support the broader cognitive conclusions.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Appendix I.1 defines gradients of a projected hidden activation with respect to input embeddings, whereas the main text describes gradients of tokens with respect to layer neurons. The projection vector and the mapping from input-space gradients to intervention sites are insufficiently specified. Confidence-interval and significance calculations also need to account explicitly for repeated observations sharing target features and prompts.

The neuron-level analysis lacks controls needed to attribute sensitivity specifically to polysemanticity. Counting connections above a fixed threshold can reflect weight scale and general neuron importance, while multiplicative amplification depends on baseline activation magnitude. Matched controls for these factors and perturbation magnitude are needed before concluding that highly polysemantic neurons are intrinsically more vulnerable.
